children: As the industry pushes for faster execution on destinations, investment, infrastructure, skilling and regulatory reform, HAI says the next phase of India’s tourism growth must focus on delivery
India’s tourism story has reached a point where ambition is no longer the central question. The harder question is whether that ambition can translate into results on the ground.

That was the central message from a press conference held alongside the 7th Hotelier’s Conclave at Taj Palace, New Delhi. K.B. Kachru, President, Hotel Association of India and Chairman – South Asia, Radisson Hotel Group; M.P.

Bezbaruah, Secretary General, Hotel Association of India; and Rohit Khosla, Vice President, Hotel Association of India and Executive Vice President (Operations), The Indian Hotels Company Limited, outlined the industry’s priorities across destination development, investment, infrastructure, employment, skilling, sustainability and regulatory reform.

The discussion came against the backdrop of the Union Budget 2025-26 identifying tourism as a sector for employment-led growth and announcing the development of the top 50 tourist destinations in partnership with states through challenge mode.
For HAI, the issue now is implementation.

“There is a gap between the vision, policy, and the realities on the ground,” Kachru said. He pointed to tourism being identified as a national growth pillar since 2014, but argued that infrastructure, connectivity and long-awaited policy changes have not kept pace with the stated ambition.

“Tourism has been recognised as one of the pillars in the Prime Minister's first speech after taking over in 2014, the first-ever independent speech; he also mentioned tourism as one of the keys, five pillars that will drive the growth of the country. But in the last 12 years, we haven’t seen that converting into, you know, tangible actions on the part of the government, of course, on the infrastructure front, connectivity front and all that. There may be some actions. But overall, on the policy changes that the industry has been looking for, that hasn’t happened so far,” Kachru said.
Destination management and workforce
Bezbaruah said tourism development cannot be measured only through hotel rooms and infrastructure, arguing that destination management must receive equal priority.

“Everything which will connect the dots is destination management. When people come to the country, they must go back with some experiences because you can build rooms, can build roads, you can build the major infrastructure. Whether he is an Indian or an overseas traveler, he goes back with an impression which can either send more people or better people from coming to India. So destination management should be an equal priority from our point of view.”
Skilling was another major concern, with HAI advocating stronger public-private partnerships using existing government infrastructure, industry trainers and apprenticeships.
“An important thing about skilling is not having a facility; you have to have students. So the outreach is also very important,” Khosla said.
Kachru also stressed that training must evolve with changing employee and guest expectations, particularly as the industry prepares for significant employment growth.
Supply, investment and industry status

HAI linked tourism expansion directly to hotel supply. Bezbaruah said prolonged restrictions on hotel development had contributed to accommodation shortages. “For literally over two decades or three decades, nothing was coming up. And no zones were created for hotels, whether it is Delhi, whether it’s Mumbai, nothing came up, which resulted in shortage of accommodation.”

On tourism being declared an industry by 17 states, Kachru said implementation remained the missing piece. “17 states have declared tourism as an industry. Great. We are very happy. All associations,  worked hard for it and it was a collaborative effort of all the associations together. But the real benefits of industry status have come only from two states.”

He added, “So my message today was very clear to our own people in the industry, and to government officials: please deliver what you have promised. We are not asking for subsidies, we are not asking for any special benefits. We are saying, give you have and include industry to monitor, to help you monitor.

“You have given us industry status. Please give us what you give to automobile, what you give to textiles, what you give to somebody else. Give us the same. We are not asking for anything extra. So if you have announced, deliver.”

For HAI, the next phase of India’s tourism growth will therefore depend less on announcing ambition and more on creating the infrastructure, investment environment, workforce and destination ecosystem required to deliver it.

The industry also used the conference to press for faster government action on several long-standing tourism issues. HAI called for the proposed 50 tourism destinations to move from announcement to implementation, questioning the delay in finalising them and arguing that each destination should be backed by the infrastructure, connectivity and investment conditions needed to make it viable. It also urged states to deliver the benefits promised under tourism industry status, including those relating to electricity, gas, licences, operational costs and infrastructure. “Please deliver what you have promised,” the association said, stressing that it was seeking implementation rather than subsidies or special treatment.

Regulatory fragmentation was another key concern raised by the industry. HAI called for greater harmonisation of tourism-related rules across states, including licensing, electricity classifications, development norms and homestay regulations, saying investors need greater clarity before committing capital to new destinations. The association also stressed that destination development cannot stop at building hotels and infrastructure. Better air and last-mile connectivity, destination management and the overall visitor experience need to be developed alongside hotel capacity, particularly as the industry looks towards Tier-II and Tier-III cities.

HAI further called for greater industry participation in monitoring the implementation of tourism policies. The association argued that the industry should not only be consulted while policies are being framed but should also be involved in tracking whether announced measures are reaching the ground. “Give us what you have and include industry to monitor, to help you monitor,” the speakers said. The broader message from the conference was that the next phase of India's tourism growth needs closer government-industry coordination, faster execution and clearer accountability for delivering what has already been announced.
